# In Praise of Things That Work

Most of what holds up a day is invisible, and it stays invisible because it succeeds.

Consider the water that comes out of a tap. Somewhere, a person you will never meet decided how wide a pipe should be, and someone else checked the pressure at a junction under a street you walk without thinking. The water is clean because thousands of small, dull, repeated acts of care happened correctly. If they hadn't, you'd notice at once. Since they did, you notice nothing at all.

I find this quietly moving. Failure is loud and gets stories written about it. Competence is silent and gets no ceremony. A bridge that stands for a hundred years is, in a sense, a hundred years of nothing happening, and that nothing was hard-won.

The same is true of small human things. A friend who always remembers to text after your hard appointment. The colleague who writes documentation nobody thanks them for, until the day it saves someone a weekend. The person who puts the shopping cart back. None of it is dramatic, but it adds up to the difference between a world that is livable and one that merely functions on paper.

I think this shapes how we tend to see value. We are drawn to the origin story, the breakthrough, the rescue. But the rescue is only needed when maintenance has failed. There's a kind of wisdom in valuing the person who prevents the fire over the person who fights it, even though only the second gets photographed.

Language works this way too. When a sentence is clear, you don't see the sentence. You see the idea, as if you'd thought it yourself. The best prose is a clean window. It took a great deal of labor to make it look like nothing was there. Writers know that the highest compliment is sometimes not "beautiful!" but "of course," the feeling that the thing could only have been said that way.

So here is my small, unglamorous suggestion for the week: notice one thing that works. A hinge that doesn't squeak, a train that arrived, a stranger who held a door. Let it be visible for a moment. Attention is a way of saying thank you when no one has given you an address to send it to.

Then go back to not noticing, which is, after all, what the good things were designed to let you do.
